DOI: [10.7554/eLife.98489.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.98489.3.sa2)

Summary:

In this work, the authors propose an extension to some of the last author's previous work, where a compositional restricted Boltzmann machine was considered as a generative model of neuron-assembly interaction. They augment this model by recurrent connections between the Boltzmann machine's hidden units, which allow them to explicitly account for temporal dynamics of the assembly activity. Since their model formulation does not allow the training towards a compositional phase (as in the previous model), they employ a transfer learning approach according to which they initialise their model with a weight matrix that was pre-trained using the earlier model so as to essentially start the actually training in a compositional phase. Finally, they test this model on synthetic and actual data of whole-brain light-sheet-microscopy recordings of spontaneous activity from the brain of larval zebrafish.

Strengths:

This work introduces a new model for neural assembly activity. Importantly, being able to capture temporal assembly dynamics is an interesting feature that goes beyond many existing models. While this work clearly focuses on the method (or the model) itself, it opens up an avenue for experimental research where it will be interesting to see if one can obtain any biologically meaningful insights considering these temporal dynamics when one is able to, for instance, relate them to development or behaviour.

Weaknesses:

For most of the work, the authors present their RTRBM model as an improvement over the earlier cRBM model. Yet, when considering synthetic data, they actually seem to compare with a "standard" RBM model. This seems odd considering the overall narrative and that when considering whole-brain zebrafish data, the comparisons were made between RTRBM and cRBM models. For that, the RTRBM model was initialised with the cRBM weight matrix to overcome the fact that RTRBM alone does not seem to converge to a compositional phase, so to cite the latter as reason does not really make sense.

Furthermore, whether the clusters shown in Figure 3E can indeed be described as "spatially localized" is debatable. Especially in view of clusters 3 and 4, this seems a stretch. If receptive fields are described as "spatially localized", arguably, one would expect that they are contained in some small (compared to the overall size of the brain) or specific anatomical brain region. However, this is clearly not the case here.

In addition, the performance comparison for the temporal dynamics of the hidden units actually suggests that the RTRBM (significantly) underperforms where the text says (Line 235f) it outperforms the cRBM model.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative performance results throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: The resulting temporal connectivity structure on the assembly level provides a compact description of the neural dynamics, which decomposes into dynamical networks of assemblies.
claims.source: The resulting temporal connectivity structure on the assembly level provides a compact description of the neural dynamics, which decomposes into dynamical networks of assemblies.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the clustering analysis shown in Figure 3D-E.

claims.claim: Training of an RTRBM/cRBM model can be completed in a few hours on current hardware.
claims.source: Training of an RTRBM/cRBM model can be completed in a few hours on current hardware, and could thus lend itself for within experiment, interventional studies.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on empirical observations of training time.

claims.claim: Estimating functional divisions and connectivity from large-scale activity data can be considered one of the key objectives of computational neuroscience.
claims.source: Estimating functional divisions and connectivity from large-scale activity data can be considered one of the key objectives of computational neuroscience, as it would allow to automatically extract interpretable structure from datasets of (human-level) uninterpretable complexity.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established understanding of computational neuroscience goals.

claims.claim: Whole-brain recordings have brought a critical advance to the endeavor of estimating functional divisions and connectivity.
claims.source: While it is generally recognized that this poses a difficult analytical challenge, in particular in highly connected systems (Das and Fiete, 2020), whole-brain recordings have brought a critical advance to this endeavor.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on citation and general knowledge about the impact of whole-brain recording technologies.

claims.claim: Surprisingly few studies exist in zebrafish that have attempted the investigation of neural activity at the whole-brain scale.
claims.source: However, due to the relatively recent introduction of whole-brain measurements in zebrafish larvae (Ahrens et al., 2013), surprisingly few studies exist in this system that have attempted the investigation of neural activity in this type of data at the whole-brain scale (Nguyen et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2018; Betzel, 2020; van der Plas et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on a review of the literature with citations to relevant studies.

claims.claim: Previous studies on whole-brain zebrafish data have focused on extracting functional groupings from neural activity without directly attempting to perform temporal predictions of neural activity.
claims.source: These studies have all focused on extracting functional groupings from the neural activity, without directly attempting to perform temporal predictions of neural activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on a review of the cited literature.

claims.claim: The current temporal resolution of light-sheet imaging is limited to a few volumes per second.
claims.source: Since the current temporal resolution of light-sheet imaging is rather low, i.e., limited of a few volumes per second (but alternative scanning approaches might change this soon, see e.g., Bouchard et al., 2015), estimating the temporal dynamics on the level of individual neurons is still difficult.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of current imaging technology limitations with citation.

claims.claim: Neural assemblies are expected to develop on slower timescales than individual neurons.
claims.source: Since the current temporal resolution of light-sheet imaging is rather low, i.e., limited of a few volumes per second (but alternative scanning approaches might change this soon, see e.g., Bouchard et al., 2015), estimating the temporal dynamics on the level of individual neurons is still difficult. Therefore, our present approach focuses on the dynamics between assemblies, which are expected to develop on slower timescales.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the justification for focusing on assembly-level dynamics.

claims.claim: Temporal connections are generally more insightful than instantaneous functional connections, as they are directed and therefore provide a better basis for separating correlation from causation.
claims.source: Temporal connections are generally more insightful than instantaneous function connections, as they are directed and therefore provide a better basis for separating correlation from causation.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about the advantages of directed temporal connections.

claims.claim: The RTRBM was able to capture functional temporal connections between neural assemblies while maintaining localized receptive fields of the hidden units.
claims.source: We demonstrate that the RTRBM was able to capture functional temporal connections between neural assemblies while maintaining localized receptive fields of the hidden units.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the results shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The RTRBM provides a way of identifying which assemblies are similar in their dynamics and thereby can suggest distinct large-scale dynamical networks spanning one or multiple brain areas.
claims.source: Additionally, as the RTRBM yields insight into the temporal dynamics of these identified neural assemblies, it provides a way of identifying which assemblies are similar in their dynamics and thereby can suggest distinct large-scale dynamical networks spanning one or multiple brain areas (see Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the clustering analysis shown in Figure 3D-E.

claims.claim: The RTRBM outperforms the classical RBM on artificial data in terms of reconstruction statistics.
claims.source: Moreover, the RTRBM outperforms the classical RBM on the artificial data in terms of reconstruction statistics, and also outperforms cRBM in accounting for temporal dynamics.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative results in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Only two earlier studies have attempted to predict dynamics or estimate dynamical relations between neural assemblies on the whole brain level in zebrafish.
claims.source: To our knowledge, only two earlier studies have attempted to predict dynamics or estimate dynamical relations between neural assemblies on the whole brain level (Watanakeesuntorn et al., 2020; Pao et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on a review of the literature with citations.

claims.claim: The RTRBM introduces temporal dependencies in a constrained way that effectively limits the number of additional parameters.
claims.source: The RTRBM introduces temporal dependencies in a constrained way that effectively limit the number of additional parameters.
claims.evidence: This claim describes a structural property of the RTRBM model.

claims.claim: Limiting the number of additional parameters is important to avoid overfitting on the limited amount of data generally available in each experiment.
claims.source: This feature is important to avoid overfitting on the limited amount of data generally available in each experiment.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about machine learning and overfitting.

claims.claim: The increased complexity involved with the addition of temporal dependencies limits the analytical tractability of the RTRBM model.
claims.source: However, the increased complexity involved with the addition of these temporal dependencies limits the analytical tractability of the model.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the mathematical properties of the RTRBM.

claims.claim: The RTRBM in its current form is not intrinsically driven toward the compositional phase.
claims.source: Specifically, the RTRBM in its current form is not intrinsically driven toward the compositional phase, which is an important property that pushes the model to identify localized neural assemblies.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on empirical observations during model development.

claims.claim: The use of dReLU hidden unit potentials within the RTRBM framework was not analytically tractable.
claims.source: Specifically, the use of dReLU hidden unit potentials within the RTRBM framework was not analytically tractable in our hands.
claims.evidence: This claim reports a technical limitation encountered during model development.

claims.claim: The cRBM-estimated assembly structure could contain an amalgam of static and dynamic connectivities.
claims.source: This approach could be limiting in multiple ways. For example, the cRBM-estimated assembly structure could contain an amalgam of static and dynamic connectivities (see Figure 2 for simulated data).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the results shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: It might be necessary to estimate the assembly structure jointly with the temporal connectivities between them for optimal decomposition.
claims.source: Furthermore, it might be necessary to estimate the assembly structure jointly with the temporal connectivities between them for optimal decomposition.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative about potential improvements to the method.

claims.claim: Another limitation of the current RTRBM framework is that all assemblies are interacting on a single time-scale.
claims.source: Another limitation of the current RTRBM framework is that all assemblies are interacting on a single time-scale.
claims.evidence: This claim describes a structural limitation of the current RTRBM implementation.

claims.claim: A single time-scale can be identified through the estimation of and subsequent selection from multiple RTRBMs on different timescales.
claims.source: While we have demonstrated (Figure 4) that a single time-scale can be identified through the estimation of and subsequent selection from multiple RTRBMs on different timescales, the more general case of multiple interaction time-scales between different assembles remains unaddressed.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the down-sampling analysis in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The estimated RTRBM generates alternating dynamics between clusters of assemblies on time-scales that are much longer than the single interaction step.
claims.source: In preliminary explorations we noticed that the estimated RTRBM generates alternating dynamics between clusters of assemblies (see Figure 3) on time-scales that are much longer than the single interaction step.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on preliminary observations from the clustering analysis.

claims.claim: Light-sheet imaging is currently limited to ∼100 Hz, which means that the ∼30–40 imaging planes are sampled at only 2–4 Hz.
claims.source: Related to the time-scale issue, light-sheet imaging is currently limited to ∼100 Hz, which means that the ∼30–40 imaging planes are sampled at only 2–4 Hz, depending on the specific system.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of current imaging technology specifications.

claims.claim: At low imaging rates it is likely that some assembly dynamics are missed or appear simultaneous.
claims.source: At these low imaging rates it is likely that some assembly dynamics are missed or appear simultaneous.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the consequences of low sampling rates.

claims.claim: Improvements in the speed of stepping between imaging planes will increase the sampling rate per cell.
claims.source: Improvements in the speed of stepping between imaging planes will increase the sampling rate per cell.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative about future technological improvements.

claims.claim: The RTRBM formalism is the logical next step in the analysis of whole-brain recordings, as it accounts for the static and dynamic aspects using a probabilistic formalism.
claims.source: The RTRBM formalism is the logical next step in the analysis of whole-brain recordings, as it accounts for the static and dynamic aspects using a probabilistic formalism, which captures both the stochastic and deterministic aspects that are hallmarks of neural activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference about the advantages of the RTRBM approach.

claims.claim: Followup studies need to attempt to extend the RTRBM into the compositional phase directly.
claims.source: Followup studies need to attempt to extend the RTRBM into the compositional phase directly, thus speeding up learning and ensuring matched assemblies and temporal connectivities (Bargmann and Marder, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative about future research directions.

claims.claim: Recordings at higher temporal resolutions and for longer durations will be instrumental in allowing convergence of the cRTRBM.
claims.source: Recordings at higher temporal resolutions and for longer durations will be instrumental in allowing convergence of the cRTRBM (Helmstaedter, 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative about future experimental improvements with citation.

claims.claim: Advancements in computing hardware should allow for interventional studies based on the estimated dynamics to directly verify the estimated temporal connectivity through modulation techniques.
claims.source: Together with advancements in computing hardware this should allow for interventional studies based on the estimated dynamics to directly verify the estimated temporal connectivity through modulation techniques such as optogenetic control or laser ablation.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative about future applications of the method.

results.result: The RTRBM extends the RBM by adding recurrent temporal connections between hidden units, allowing it to model temporal dependencies between neural assemblies while maintaining the probabilistic and interpretable features of the RBM.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16, C24, and C28 collectively describe the architectural properties of the RTRBM as an extension of the RBM with temporal connections. These are well-established structural properties of the model supported by citations and are consistent with the mathematical formulation presented in the methods.

results.result: On simulated data with known temporal structure, the RTRBM successfully recovers the true assembly-to-neuron weights and temporal connections, outperforming the RBM in capturing time-shifted moments while performing comparably on simultaneous moments.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19, C30-C31, C35-C36, C40-C41 are supported by the simulated data experiments shown in Figure 2. The RTRBM correctly identifies the diagonal weight structure and temporal connections, with statistically significant improvements in time-shifted moments (p<0.001) while maintaining similar performance on concurrent statistics.

results.result: Transfer learning from cRBM to RTRBM successfully maintains localized neural assemblies while adding temporal connections on whole-brain zebrafish data, with training converging successfully for all animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C21, C44, C46, C49, and C61 describe the transfer learning methodology and its outcomes. The approach is well-documented with evidence of successful training convergence and maintenance of sparse weight distributions (Figure 3B-C), supporting the claim that localized assemblies are preserved.

results.result: The RTRBM outperforms the cRBM on zebrafish data in terms of reconstructing first-order, second-order, and time-shifted moments, with improvements observed in the majority of animals tested.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C57, C59-C60, and C69 are supported by the comparative analysis in Figure 3F-G showing lower sum square differences and higher Spearman correlations for RTRBM across multiple statistical measures. The RTRBM outperformed cRBM on 4-6 out of 8 fish for different moment types, with bootstrap-based significance testing.

results.result: The RTRBM identifies spatially localized neural assemblies that cluster into distinct dynamical networks based on their temporal connectivity patterns, providing a compact description of neural dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C70, C79-C80 are supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 3D-E. Agglomerative clustering on the temporal weight matrix U reveals distinct clusters with characteristic connectivity patterns, and the corresponding receptive fields show spatial localization.

results.result: The optimal temporal resolution for RTRBM modeling can be identified by training multiple RTRBMs at different down-sampling rates and comparing their performance, with the natural sampling rate showing highest correlation for zebrafish data.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C62-C63, C67, and C91 are supported by the down-sampling analysis in Figure 4. For simulated data, performance peaked when down-sampling matched the true interaction time (Δt=4), and for zebrafish data, the natural sampling rate yielded highest Spearman correlations (Figure 4E).

results.result: The RTRBM demonstrates functional advantages captured in temporal weights on hidden units for both simulated and experimental data, outperforming the stochastic-only cRBM in generalization error and temporal moment representation.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3 and C68 summarize the main findings supported by results throughout the manuscript. The temporal weights U successfully capture dynamics in both simulated (Figure 2) and zebrafish data (Figure 3), with quantitative improvements in generalization error and moment reconstruction.

results.result: The RTRBM in its current form does not intrinsically reach the compositional phase, and the use of dReLU hidden unit potentials within the RTRBM framework was not analytically tractable.
results.evaluation: Claims C29, C86-C87 report empirical limitations encountered during model development. These are honest assessments of technical challenges that motivated the transfer learning approach, and are consistent with the methodological choices described.

results.result: The transfer learning approach may be limiting because the cRBM-estimated assembly structure could contain an amalgam of static and dynamic connectivities, and joint estimation of assembly structure with temporal connectivities might be necessary for optimal decomposition.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 identify potential limitations of the transfer learning approach. While C88 references Figure 2 showing the RBM conflates static and dynamic connections, the extent to which this affects the final RTRBM results on real data is not directly tested. C89 is speculative about future improvements.

results.result: The current RTRBM framework assumes all assemblies interact on a single time-scale, though preliminary observations suggest the model generates alternating dynamics between clusters on longer timescales than the single interaction step.
results.evaluation: Claims C90 and C92 describe a structural limitation (single time-scale) and preliminary observations of longer-timescale dynamics. C90 is a clear limitation of the model architecture, and C92 is supported by preliminary observations from Figure 3, though this is acknowledged as exploratory.

results.result: Training of an RTRBM/cRBM model can be completed in a few hours on current hardware.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 is supported by empirical observations stated in the methods section, where training for 10,000 epochs took approximately 3 hours on an NVIDIA RTX3090 GPU. This is a practical consideration for the feasibility of the method.

results.result: The cRBM, an extension of the RBM, can decompose whole-brain zebrafish activity into ~100-200 localized assemblies with sparse connections, but is limited to capturing only static dependencies without temporal dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C12 describe prior work on the cRBM (van der Plas et al., 2023) and its known limitations. These are well-supported by citations to previous work and established knowledge about the model architecture, providing context for the current study.

results.result: Neural assemblies are thought to be elementary computational units essential for cognitive functions, and while light-sheet microscopy enables whole-brain recordings, extracting activation patterns from ~100,000+ neurons remains computationally challenging, requiring explicit modeling of both stochastic and deterministic dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 and C13 provide background context supported by citations to established literature (Harris, 2005; Hebb, 1949; Ahrens et al., 2013) and general knowledge about computational neuroscience challenges. These claims establish the motivation for the study.

results.result: Previous studies using RTRBMs in other domains have shown value in extracting spatiotemporal features, and while estimating functional connectivity from large-scale data is a key objective in computational neuroscience, surprisingly few studies have attempted temporal prediction of neural activity at the whole-brain scale in zebrafish.
results.evaluation: Claims C17, C72-C75, and C82 provide literature context supported by multiple citations. The review of prior work accurately characterizes the state of the field and positions the current work within it, though the accuracy of the literature characterization depends on the cited sources.

results.result: Current light-sheet imaging is limited to a few volumes per second (2-4 Hz for 30-40 planes), making individual neuron dynamics difficult to estimate, but assembly-level dynamics are expected to develop on slower timescales, and temporal connections provide better basis for separating correlation from causation than instantaneous connections.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78, C93-C94 describe technical limitations of current imaging technology and their implications. These are supported by citations and general knowledge about imaging constraints, providing reasonable justification for focusing on assembly-level rather than single-neuron dynamics.

results.result: The RTRBM outperforms the classical RBM on artificial data in terms of reconstruction statistics and outperforms cRBM in accounting for temporal dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 summarizes comparative results supported by Figure 2 (RTRBM vs RBM on simulated data) and Figure 3 (RTRBM vs cRBM on zebrafish data). The claim is well-supported by the quantitative comparisons presented throughout the results.

results.result: The RTRBM introduces temporal dependencies in a constrained way that limits additional parameters to avoid overfitting, but the increased complexity limits analytical tractability of the model.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 describe design trade-offs in the RTRBM architecture. These are based on the mathematical structure of the model and general machine learning principles about overfitting and model complexity, representing honest assessment of the approach.

results.result: The RTRBM can realize a combination of temporal sequences and stochastic exploration.
results.evaluation: Claim C26 is demonstrated by the sampling results shown in Figure 1F, where the RTRBM generates activity traces showing sequential activation patterns combined with stochastic variability, in contrast to the purely stochastic RBM samples.

results.result: Future improvements in imaging speed and computing hardware, along with extending the RTRBM to the compositional phase and using higher temporal resolution recordings, should enable interventional studies to verify estimated temporal connectivity through optogenetic control or laser ablation.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99 are speculative about future work and technological improvements. While these represent reasonable directions for future research, they are not tested in the current study and depend on technological advances and methodological developments that have not yet been demonstrated.

results.result: The RTRBM successfully retrieves artificial neural assemblies and their temporal connections in simulated data, outperforming the standard RBM in terms of generalization error, pairwise moments, and particularly time-shifted moments. The RBM recovers non-diagonal weight matrices that partially account for dependencies but cannot accurately capture time-shifted moments.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states the authors 'show solid evidence that the new model outperforms their earlier model on both a simulated dataset and on whole-brain neural activity from zebrafish.' Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'the analysis is solid to support the authors claim.' The simulated data results are not challenged by any reviewer.

results.result: The RTRBM extension outperforms the cRBM in terms of generalization error and provides more accurate representation of moments in time on zebrafish data, with lower sum square difference for first-, second-, and time-shifted moments, though performance varies across individual fish.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'the performance improvement by RTRBM compared to their cRBM is marginal' and Reviewer 3 states 'the performance comparison for the temporal dynamics of the hidden units actually suggests that the RTRBM (significantly) underperforms where the text says (Line 235f) it outperforms the cRBM model.' This directly contradicts the authors' claims of superior performance.

results.result: The trained RTRBM model maintained localized neural assemblies inherited from the cRBM, with sparse weight distributions and spatially localized sets of neurons forming clusters.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly challenges this claim, stating 'whether the clusters shown in Figure 3E can indeed be described as "spatially localized" is debatable. Especially in view of clusters 3 and 4, this seems a stretch.' The reviewer argues that truly localized receptive fields should be 'contained in some small (compared to the overall size of the brain) or specific anatomical brain region,' which is 'clearly not the case here.'

results.result: Transfer learning was used to initialize RTRBM weights with cRBM counterparts because the RTRBM did not reach the compositional phase directly. This approach successfully expanded the cRBM model to include temporal connections while maintaining sparsity.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 questions the methodological consistency, noting 'when considering synthetic data, they actually seem to compare with a "standard" RBM model' rather than cRBM, which 'seems odd considering the overall narrative.' The reviewer states that citing inability to reach compositional phase as justification 'does not really make sense' given the transfer learning workaround was used for zebrafish data.

results.result: The RTRBM captures temporal dependencies between neural assemblies through temporal weights on hidden units, providing a compact description of neural dynamics that decomposes into dynamical networks of assemblies spanning brain areas.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 questions the biological value, stating 'the biological insights from this method are constrained' and asks 'What information can we gain by knowing the effective recurrent connection between them?' The reviewer suggests 'dynamics of assemblies can be analyzed using various tools such as dimensionality reduction methods once we have identified them using cRBM,' questioning the unique contribution of RTRBM.

results.result: The original time-scale of assembly dynamics can be identified by estimating multiple RTRBMs at different temporal resolutions, with the Spearman correlation of moments being highest at the natural sampling rate for zebrafish data.
results.evaluation: This methodological contribution is not challenged by any reviewer. Reviewer 1 acknowledges the authors 'show solid evidence' for their model's capabilities, which would include this temporal resolution analysis presented in Figure 4.

results.result: The RTRBM maintains interpretable and probabilistic features of the RBM while extending it to include temporal dependencies, allowing the model to realize a combination of temporal sequences and stochastic exploration that the static cRBM cannot capture.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 describes this as 'a useful extension to a recently proposed model' and Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'being able to capture temporal assembly dynamics is an interesting feature that goes beyond many existing models.' The conceptual advance is accepted even if practical benefits are questioned.

results.result: Individual fluorescence traces were successfully deconvolved using blind sparse deconvolution to obtain binarized spike traces, and model training converged successfully for each animal.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 requests 'predicted and measured neural activity traces could aid readers in evaluating model efficacy' but does not challenge the preprocessing methodology itself. The successful training is not disputed by any reviewer.

results.result: The cRBM is limited to capturing only static dependencies and cannot account for temporal dependencies, while neural activity driving behavior requires explicit dynamics. Current light-sheet imaging temporal resolution limits individual neuron dynamics estimation, making assembly-level temporal connections more tractable and insightful.
results.evaluation: These motivational claims about limitations of static models and advantages of temporal approaches are not challenged by reviewers. Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'most of previous studies do not explicit modeling the temporal dynamics' and this study addresses that gap.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting 'marginal' improvements and one reviewer claiming RTRBM 'significantly underperforms' on temporal dynamics. Major disagreement on zebrafish performance.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, explicitly challenging whether clusters are 'spatially localized,' calling it 'a stretch' especially for clusters 3 and 4. Significant disagreement.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, questioning biological value and suggesting alternative methods could achieve similar insights. Disagreement on significance of contribution.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, questioning methodological consistency and why cRBM wasn't used for synthetic data comparison. Disagreement on methodological choices.
